Specialist Therapeutic Education for Children and Young People
Every child deserves a school where they feel understood
For many families, finding the right school starts with a simple hope: that their child will feel safe, happy and able to succeed. Compass Community Schools provide specialist education for children and young people with special educational needs, autism, SEMH needs and other barriers to learning through therapeutic support, personalised learning and trusted relationships. We help children build a future they never thought possible.
Looking for an SEN school near you?
Compass Community Schools operate specialist schools across England supporting children and young people with a range of additional needs. Use our school finder to explore locations, age ranges and specialist support available near you.
A school built around your child
Small Classes
Maximum six students per class.
Therapeutic Support
Wellbeing and emotional development alongside education.
Personalised Learning
Education adapted around the individual child.
"My child's very happy there now, in mainstream they were in crisis."
Compass Schools Parent
Supporting children with a wide range of needs

From first day to future success
Feeling Safe: James’s Story
When James first arrived, he wasn’t sure what to expect. Like many children, he was anxious about whether this school would be any different. With shorter days, plenty of time to settle in, and staff who took the time to listen, James began to feel safe, understood and accepted. The first small steps had begun.
Building Trust: Oscar’s Story
Oscar joined Compass struggling to communicate and connect with others. Staff looked beyond his behaviour and took the time to understand him as a person. As relationships grew, so did trust. For the first time, Oscar and his family felt that people could see his strengths, not just his challenges.
Growing Confidence: Aysha’s Story
When loud noises made school difficult, Aysha’s teacher took the time to listen and help her find ways to manage her anxiety. With patience, understanding and the right support, Aysha grew in confidence. She became more able to cope with challenging situations and began to succeed in her education.
Looking Ahead
When children feel safe, build trust and grow in confidence, they begin to believe in themselves. Children like James, Oscar and Aysha start to look ahead with excitement to what comes next – gaining qualifications, developing life skills, building friendships and preparing for college, work and greater independence.
Building futures, not just qualifications
At Compass Schools, we help young people achieve recognised qualifications while preparing for life beyond school. Alongside GCSEs and vocational qualifications, pupils develop practical skills through subjects such as construction, hair and beauty, hospitality, outdoor learning and animal care. We also focus on the things that matter every day – building confidence, forming positive friendships, managing emotions and growing in independence. Whether it’s gaining qualifications, learning new skills or preparing for college, work and adult life, every step helps young people build a future they can look forward to with confidence.
What makes Compass different?
At Compass Schools, we know that every child is different. That’s why we keep our class sizes small, so pupils get the support they need to succeed. Our caring, therapeutic approach helps young people feel safe, settled and ready to learn. With specialist staff and a personalised curriculum, learning is tailored to each child’s strengths and needs. As part of a national network of specialist schools, we combine local care with shared expertise and proven approaches. The result is strong outcomes that help pupils build confidence, achieve their goals and look forward to a positive future.
Find your nearest Compass Community School
Whether you're looking for an SEN school, special school, SEMH school or specialist provision for your child, our team can help you find the right Compass school near you.
An SEN (Special Educational Needs) school is a specialist school that supports children and young people whose needs cannot always be fully met in a mainstream setting. SEN schools provide tailored teaching, specialist staff, therapeutic support and personalised learning programmes designed around each child’s individual strengths, challenges and goals. Compass Community Schools support pupils with a range of needs, including autism, social, emotional and mental health (SEMH) needs, anxiety, communication difficulties and other barriers to learning. Small class sizes, therapeutic approaches and personalised education help pupils feel safe, build confidence and achieve positive outcomes both academically and personally.
Compass Community Schools support children and young people who need a more specialist educational environment than mainstream schools can provide. Many pupils have an Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP), autism, SEMH needs, anxiety, attendance difficulties or other additional needs that affect their ability to access learning. Every child is different. Some pupils may have struggled with school attendance, experienced trauma, found large classrooms overwhelming or require a more personalised approach to learning. Compass schools focus on understanding each child as an individual and providing the support they need to feel safe, succeed and prepare for the future.
Yes. All pupils attending Compass Community Schools have an Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP). Compass schools work closely with local authorities, families and professionals to ensure that the provision outlined in a child’s EHCP can be delivered effectively. Each placement is considered individually to ensure the school can meet the child’s educational, social, emotional and therapeutic needs. Families are encouraged to contact the team to discuss their child’s circumstances and explore suitable options.
Yes. Compass Community Schools support autistic children and young people through personalised learning, structured environments and therapeutic approaches that help pupils feel understood and able to learn successfully. Support may include smaller class sizes, predictable routines, sensory considerations, communication support and individual learning plans tailored to each pupil’s strengths and needs. Staff take time to build trusted relationships and create an environment where autistic pupils can develop confidence, independence and academic success.
Compass Community Schools provide specialist support for children and young people with Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH) needs. Education is delivered alongside therapeutic support to help pupils understand emotions, develop resilience, improve wellbeing and build positive relationships. Support may include therapeutic interventions, emotional regulation strategies, pastoral care, personalised behaviour support and opportunities to develop confidence and self-esteem. The goal is to help pupils feel safe, engage positively with learning and achieve long-term success both in school and beyond.
You can use the Compass Community Schools school finder to search for specialist schools near you. Compass operates schools across England, supporting children and young people with autism, SEMH needs, EHCPs and other additional needs. The school finder allows families and professionals to explore locations, age ranges and specialist support available at each school. If you’re unsure which school may be suitable, the Compass team can help guide you through the options and answer any questions about placements and referrals.
Yes. Compass Community Schools understand that choosing the right school is an important decision for families. Visits and discussions are encouraged wherever possible so parents, carers and professionals can learn more about the school’s environment, therapeutic approach and support available. A visit provides an opportunity to meet staff, ask questions and explore whether the school is the right fit for your child. Families can contact the Compass team directly to discuss next steps and arrange a conversation about their child’s needs.

You don't need all the answers today. The first step is simply a conversation.

pageCache.pageTitle: Is a SEN School Right for My Child? | Parent Guide
pageCache.text:
Is A SEN School The Right Choice For My Child?
A SEN school can be the right choice when a child needs more specialist, personalised support than a mainstream setting can consistently provide. Smaller classes, staff who understand special educational needs, therapeutic support and a curriculum shaped around the individual can help children feel safe, enjoy school again and make meaningful progress.
Choosing a school is still a personal decision. The best setting is not defined by a label; it is the one that understands your child, meets the needs set out in their Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP), and gives them genuine opportunities to learn, build relationships and prepare for the future.
What is a SEN school?
A SEN school—also called a special school or specialist school—provides education for children and young people whose special educational needs require more targeted support. Pupils may have needs associated with autism, social, emotional and mental health (SEMH), communication, cognition and learning, sensory processing, anxiety or experiences that have made it difficult to engage with education.
Different specialist schools support different profiles of need, age ranges and levels of ability. That is why the right question is not simply whether a SEN school is ‘better’ than a mainstream school, but whether a particular school is the right match for your child.
What are the benefits of a SEN school?
Smaller classes and more individual attention
Smaller classes give staff more time to get to know each pupil: how they communicate, what helps them feel settled, where their strengths lie and what can make learning difficult. Teaching can then be adapted in pace, content and approach, rather than expecting every child to learn in the same way.
For many children, this creates the space to take part more confidently, ask for help and experience success without feeling lost in a busy classroom.
Specialist staff who understand SEN
In a strong SEN school, teachers and support staff understand that behaviour, anxiety, withdrawal or difficulty attending school may communicate an unmet need. They can use specialist strategies, predictable routines and trusted relationships to reduce barriers and help a child become ready to learn.
At Compass Community Schools, education and wellbeing are brought together. Teachers, therapists and specialist professionals work closely to understand each child and provide practical support around their individual needs.
Personalised learning with meaningful ambition
Specialist education should never mean lowering expectations. It means finding a realistic and motivating route towards them. A personalised curriculum can build from a pupil’s starting point while keeping sight of academic achievement, communication, independence, confidence and future opportunities.
Compass pupils can work towards recognised outcomes including GCSEs, alongside other qualifications and learning pathways where these better reflect the individual. The aim is meaningful progress—not a one-size-fits-all version of success.
Therapeutic support within the school day
Some children cannot make academic progress until they feel safe, understood and able to regulate their emotions. A therapeutic approach helps school staff respond to the needs behind behaviour and create the conditions in which learning becomes possible again.
At Compass, therapeutic thinking is embedded across school life. Our in-house Multi-Disciplinary Therapy Team can provide specialist assessment and intervention, while education staff use this understanding to support pupils consistently throughout the day. This joined-up approach can strengthen emotional wellbeing, resilience, relationships and engagement with learning.
A greater sense of belonging
Children who have felt different, misunderstood or repeatedly unsuccessful in school can begin to see themselves differently in a specialist environment. They meet peers who may share some of their experiences, while being valued for their own personality, abilities and interests.
Friendships do not happen automatically in any setting, but smaller communities and carefully supported social opportunities can make it easier for pupils to build trust, practise social skills and feel that they belong.
Closer communication with families
Parents and carers know their child in ways that no school can. Regular, honest communication helps home and school share what is working, recognise changes early and respond consistently.
At Compass Community Schools, listening to families is an important part of understanding the whole child. The strongest placements are partnerships in which parents, pupils, school staff, professionals and the local authority work towards shared goals.

None of these signs makes the decision on its own. They are prompts for a fuller conversation about what your child needs and which setting is best able to provide it.
What should families consider when comparing schools?
Every placement involves practical and personal considerations. Instead of treating these as disadvantages of SEN schools generally, look closely at how each individual school responds.
Curriculum and qualifications
Ask what subjects, qualifications and wider learning opportunities are available, and how these would be personalised for your child. A good school should be ambitious, but it should also recognise that progress can include attendance, communication, emotional regulation, relationships and independence as well as exam results.
Travel and the length of the school day
The most suitable specialist school may be further from home than the nearest mainstream school. Find out what transport may be available, how long the journey would take and how the school helps pupils settle at the beginning and end of the day. A longer journey is an important consideration, but it should be weighed against how well the placement meets your child’s needs.
Friendships and the wider community
Ask how the school supports friendships, group activities, community participation and preparation for life beyond school. A smaller specialist setting may offer a narrower peer group, but it can also provide a safer foundation from which a child develops the confidence and skills to connect with others.
Wherever possible, involve your child in visits and conversations. What helps them feel comfortable? Do staff speak to them with warmth and respect? Can they imagine themselves learning there? Their response will not answer every question, but it is an important part of the decision.
How do I choose the right SEN school?
Visit more than once if you can, and look beyond the building or prospectus. Notice the relationships between pupils and adults and ask how the school would support your child specifically.

The right school should be able to explain not only what it offers, but how that support could help your child take their next steps.
What qualifications and pathways could be available?
What makes Compass Community Schools different?
Compass Community Schools are small specialist schools that combine personalised education with a therapeutic understanding of each child. Many pupils join us after school has felt difficult, disrupted or unsafe. We take time to build trust, recognise strengths and understand what may be getting in the way of learning.
Our staff work together to create calm, supportive environments where pupils can reconnect with education.
Learning is personalised, relationships are central and ambition remains high. Alongside academic progress and qualifications, we help children and young people build confidence, friendships, emotional wellbeing and greater independence for life beyond school.
The goal is not simply to help a child cope with school. It is to help them feel understood, discover what they can achieve and develop a more positive future.
Is a SEN school the right choice for my child?
A SEN school may be the right choice if its specialist environment, teaching and support match your child’s individual needs better than their current provision. For many families, the change is not about giving something up; it is about giving their child access to the understanding, opportunities and sense of belonging they need to flourish.
Speak with your child, their SENCo, teachers and other professionals involved in their support. If your child has an EHCP, you can also discuss specialist provision and school preferences with your Local Authority. Then visit potential schools and ask how they would turn the plan on paper into a positive daily experience for your child.
Talk to Compass Community Schools
If you are considering specialist education, we would be happy to talk with you about your child’s needs and help you understand what life at a Compass Community School could look like. You can also explore our schools to find the setting nearest to you and learn more about our therapeutic approach to education.

pageCache.pageTitle: Therapeutic Education for Learning Disabilities | Compass
pageCache.text:
How Therapeutic Education Supports Children with Learning Disabilities
By Natalie Wager, Regional Therapeutic Lead at Compass Community Schools
Therapeutic education supports children with learning disabilities by bringing personalised learning, emotional support and specialist understanding together throughout the school day. At Compass Schools, we adapt teaching, communication and the environment around each child so they can feel safe, participate in learning and develop greater confidence and independence.
What is a learning disability?
A learning disability affects the way a person understands and processes information and can influence the development of new skills. Children may need additional support with communication, learning, problem-solving, independence and everyday activities.
However, a diagnosis tells us only one part of a child’s story. Every child comes to us with their own strengths, interests, experiences, ways of communicating and hopes for the future. Rather than beginning with, “What can’t this child do?”, we recognise what they can do and ask, “What do they need from us to help them move forward?”
What is the difference between a learning disability and a learning difficulty?
Although the terms are sometimes used interchangeably, they mean different things. A learning disability affects intellectual ability and can influence understanding information, learning new skills and managing aspects of everyday life. A learning difficulty affects a particular area of learning without affecting overall intellectual ability; examples include dyslexia, dyscalculia and dyspraxia.
The distinction matters, but neither term should determine what we believe a child can achieve. We support the child in front of us, not simply their diagnosis.
How can learning disabilities affect a child at school?
Every child experiences their learning disability differently. Some need more processing time, support with instructions or different ways to communicate. Others may experience challenges with social interaction, sensory processing, emotional regulation or independence.
Imagine repeatedly receiving instructions you cannot process quickly enough, being in an environment that feels overwhelming or being unable to communicate that something is wrong. Understandably, this can affect confidence, emotional wellbeing and a child’s relationship with learning.
This is why we remain curious about behaviour. Rather than asking only, “How do we stop this behaviour?”, we ask, “What might this child be communicating to us?”
Why can children with learning disabilities benefit from therapeutic education?
Children are more available for learning when they feel safe, understood and supported. Trusted relationships are especially important for children who find communication, processing or emotional regulation difficult. Consistent adults who genuinely seek to understand them can create the safety needed for learning.
At Compass Schools, therapeutic support does not happen only in a therapy room. Therapeutic thinking is part of the child’s wider experience of school within our therapeutic education model. Sometimes this means supporting regulation before returning to learning; at other times it means changing how learning is presented.
How does Compass assess each child’s individual needs?
Getting the right provision begins with understanding the child and ensuring the school can meet their needs. A child’s Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) provides an important picture of their needs and required provision, but understanding a child cannot come from paperwork alone.
Parents and carers are involved from the beginning. Their knowledge of how their child communicates, what they enjoy, what causes anxiety and what helps them regulate is invaluable. Professional assessments, communication, sensory needs, emotional wellbeing, abilities and previous education are considered alongside the child’s voice and aspirations. This understanding continues to develop as relationships form and the child settles.
How is learning personalised at Compass Schools?
Personalising learning does not mean lowering aspirations. It means finding the best way for each child to access learning. Curriculum content, pace, teaching methods, the environment and timetables can be adapted where appropriate. If something is not working, we ask why and consider another approach.
The child’s voice is central. Giving children appropriate autonomy helps us understand how they learn best and what motivates them. Learning should be something we do with a child, not something done to them.
How do Compass Schools support communication and interaction?
Communication is much more than spoken language. It is how children tell us what they want, what they enjoy, when something feels wrong and when they need help.
Education and therapeutic teams work with other professionals to understand each child’s communication needs and use appropriate strategies consistently. Children also need meaningful opportunities to make choices, express preferences and influence their education and support. A child not communicating in the way we might expect does not mean they have nothing to say.
How are sensory and emotional needs supported?
The environment can make an enormous difference to a child’s ability to participate and learn. Children can access spaces and sensory opportunities according to their needs, including soft-play areas, outdoor equipment, sand and water activities and classroom sensory resources. Used purposefully, these can support regulation and help a child become ready to engage.
I saw this first-hand during a visit to a Compass school. A child was struggling in the classroom and staff knew that, when anxious, he could begin scratching his face. His teacher recognised the early signs and, knowing how much he enjoyed water, adapted the activity and filled the water-play area.
We joined him and had a real play. We all got very wet, as did the surrounding area, but that did not matter. The water could be cleaned up; responding to what the child needed was more important.
He gradually relaxed, stopped scratching his face and became visibly calmer. Importantly, he understood that afterwards he would return to learning and he did.
For me, this is therapeutic education in practice: knowing the child, recognising what they are communicating and understanding that sometimes regulation must come before learning.
This approach can also support a child’s emotional wellbeing and engagement with education.
What role does the multidisciplinary team play?
Children’s needs do not fit neatly into separate boxes, so neither should the support around them. Team Around the Child (TAC) meetings bring together school staff, parents and carers, therapists and relevant professionals. When a child begins working with a therapist, a TAC is held after six weeks and then every 12 weeks so everyone can share observations, consider progress and ensure the child’s needs continue to be met.
For children living in a Compass children’s home, triangulation meetings connect education, therapeutic and residential teams. This collaboration means the adults around the child are working from the same page.
How do small classes and trusted relationships help?
Small classes allow adults to know the children they support: how they communicate, what makes them smile, what worries them and the subtle changes that may show something is wrong. Smaller groups can reduce overwhelm and provide manageable opportunities to develop relationships with other children and trusted adults.
Trust develops through consistency, patience and repeated experiences of adults being available and responsive. When children feel safe, they are more able to communicate, explore and take appropriate risks in their learning.
How does Compass support independence and preparation for adulthood?
Independence means something different for every child. Communication, decision-making, everyday skills, confidence and autonomy can be developed throughout their education.
As children approach GCSE age, staff work with them and their families to explore colleges, sixth forms and other suitable provision, supporting visits where needed. Successful transition also means helping the next setting understand the young person’s communication, needs and successful strategies so appropriate support can continue.
What progress and outcomes can children achieve?
Progress does not look the same for every child. Academic achievement and qualifications are important where appropriate, but progress can also be emotional, social, communicative and practical. Success might mean independently communicating a need, developing a friendship, managing a difficult transition or engaging with learning for longer.
Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEW) assessments help us understand progress beyond academic attainment. Staff, Therapeutic Pastoral Leads, therapists and other professionals can identify changes and consider areas where progress may have dipped. A dip does not mean a child has failed; it gives us information. We can ask what has changed, whether the child feels safe and whether their current support still meets their needs.
How are families involved in their child’s education?
Families are not on the outside looking in; they are part of the team around their child. Parents and carers contribute through reviews, TAC meetings, shared goals and ongoing communication. Therapeutic Pastoral Leads may also meet parents, provide drop-ins and be available during events such as parents’ evenings.
Something a parent tells us can provide the missing piece of the picture; equally, something noticed at school may help a family understand a change at home.
Ultimately, therapeutic education for children with learning disabilities is about seeing the whole child. It means looking beyond diagnosis and behaviour, remaining curious about communication, relationships, sensory needs, emotional wellbeing, strengths and aspirations, and bringing the adults around the child together.
Many children may also have social, emotional and mental health needs alongside their learning disability, requiring support that recognises the whole child.
For some children, a specialist SEN school can provide the smaller, more personalised and therapeutic environment they need.
Could a Compass school be right for your child?
When children feel safe, understood and valued, and the adults around them work together, we create the conditions in which each child can learn, develop and move towards a positive future that is meaningful to them.
You can find your nearest Compass school to learn more about our specialist provision, or contact our team to discuss your child’s needs and the provision available.

Therapeutic Education
Many of the children and young people who join our schools have experienced challenges that can affect how they learn, build relationships, and engage with education. That’s why therapeutic thinking sits at the centre of our approach. Rather than viewing education and wellbeing as separate, we bring them together to create environments where children feel safe, understood, and able to make progress. Our teachers, therapists, and specialist professionals work closely together to understand each child’s individual needs and provide support that is both meaningful and practical. This joined-up approach helps young people develop confidence, resilience, emotional wellbeing, and positive relationships alongside their academic learning. The impact of trauma is different for every child. Some young people need targeted therapeutic intervention, while others benefit from therapeutic support embedded throughout their school experience. By understanding the individual behind the behaviour, we can respond to need at the right time and in the right way. This personalised approach helps remove barriers to learning and gives children and young people the opportunity to thrive both in school and beyond.

Our innovative OCT and OST therapeutic programmes are provided by New Ways Safeguarding, an organisation dedicated to working with young people who have experienced early-life trauma.
New Ways Safeguarding was established by the leading international forensic psychologist Dr Joe Sullivan and Clinical Director Dr Valerie Sheehan and consists of a multi-disciplinary team of highly experienced practitioners. Their industry-leading services have a long history of providing a range of services and their assessment and intervention work is underpinned by the most recent research in the field as well as extensive clinical practice.

What Is Assessing and Healing Complex Trauma (AHCT)?
By Helena Dolphin, Regional Therapeutic Lead at Compass Community Schools
Assessing and Healing Complex Trauma (AHCT) is a framework used across Compass Community Schools to help us understand, assess and support children as they recover from the effects of complex trauma. It is trauma-informed and child-led, with a strong emphasis on developing safety, trust and positive relationships. At Compass Schools, we recognise that these relationships create the foundations children need to develop, learn and thrive.
What is complex trauma in children?
Complex trauma refers to repeated or prolonged traumatic experiences, particularly when they occur within relationships that should be safe, such as those with parents or carers. It is sometimes called developmental trauma because it happens during important stages of a child’s development.
Unlike a single traumatic event, complex trauma occurs over time and can affect how the brain develops and functions.
How can complex trauma affect a child?
Complex trauma can have a significant impact on development, shifting a child’s focus from learning and growth to survival.
Children may struggle with emotional regulation because they have not experienced enough co-regulation to develop these skills. Their nervous system can become highly alert to perceived danger, so they may move quickly from appearing calm to becoming overwhelmed or distressed. Others may appear withdrawn or shut down because suppressing emotions has become a way of staying safe.
Their senses may also become heightened as they scan for potential threats. This hypervigilance can be exhausting and make everyday situations feel unsafe.
Relationships can be particularly challenging. Children who have experienced complex trauma may have learned that adults are unpredictable or unsafe, making trust difficult. This can affect their relationships with adults and peers, as well as their self-esteem, confidence and decision-making.
How does complex trauma affect learning and school life?
A helpful way to think about this is to imagine the brain as an internet browser with many tabs open. Complex trauma keeps those tabs running in the background, constantly monitoring for danger. This uses valuable mental resources and leaves less capacity for learning, concentration and memory.
When much of a child’s energy is focused on staying safe, reading, writing, maths and listening can become much harder. Relationships at school may also feel challenging because adults and peers can be viewed as potential threats.
Without an understanding of trauma, behaviour can appear unpredictable. However, these behaviours are often adaptive responses developed to help the child survive difficult experiences. School may therefore become another environment that feels difficult to navigate, affecting attendance, engagement and progress.
These experiences can also affect a child’s emotional wellbeing and engagement with school.
What is the AHCT approach?
At Compass, we use AHCT to help children understand their experiences and develop a greater sense of safety, security and wellbeing.
We begin by gathering information from different sources to build a holistic picture of the child. We seek to understand their strengths, needs, history and current presentation so that support can be tailored effectively. We ask, “What has happened to this child?” rather than, “What is wrong with them?”
Assessment considers factors including trauma history, attachment, neurodiversity, cognitive functioning and development. Once needs have been identified, we develop a collaborative therapeutic plan with the child, family and relevant professionals. Together, we agree desired outcomes, identify strengths and decide how support will be delivered and reviewed.
Every member of staff at Compass receives therapeutic training. All pupils participate in weekly therapeutic group sessions led by Therapeutic Pastoral Leads, with content informed by Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEW) assessments. Many children also receive individual therapy. Therapists work alongside schools and families to develop a shared understanding of the child’s experiences and support a clear, consistent life narrative.
How are a child’s therapeutic needs assessed?
Understanding a child’s therapeutic needs involves building a picture over time. We combine existing information, professional assessments and the child’s history with what we learn through observation and everyday interactions.
We consider patterns rather than isolated incidents: when a child finds situations difficult, how they respond to adults, what helps them feel safe, how they manage change and what happens when they become overwhelmed. This helps us understand what may be driving a response rather than viewing behaviour in isolation.
The child’s perspective is central. Depending on their age, development and communication needs, this may be gathered through conversation, therapeutic work, observation or relationships with trusted adults. Parents, carers and professionals also contribute different parts of the child’s story.
SEW assessments help identify the child’s strengths and areas where further support may be needed. Therapeutic Pastoral Leads, education staff, therapists and other professionals can then consider what may sit underneath those needs and what support may be most appropriate. Assessment is not about attaching a label to behaviour; it is about developing an understanding that guides how adults respond.
How does AHCT support children in school?
AHCT is a shared approach within our wider therapeutic education model, not something delivered by one person or confined to a therapy session. Therapeutic thinking is embedded throughout a child’s school experience through:
This means therapeutic thinking is present in everyday moments: noticing when a child is becoming overwhelmed, adapting expectations, supporting regulation and repairing relationships when trust and safety have been disrupted.
Personalised therapeutic interventions tailored to individual needs.
Predictable routines that reduce uncertainty.
How do education and therapy work together?
At Compass, therapeutic support is central to everything we do, not an additional service. Education staff, therapists, families and other professionals develop a shared understanding of each child. Team Around the Child (TAC) meetings allow everyone to review progress, discuss concerns and ensure that support remains effective.
For children living in Compass children’s homes, education, residential and therapeutic teams work closely together to promote consistency across every environment. Put simply, everyone works from the same page.
Which children may benefit from AHCT?
AHCT is particularly relevant when there is a need to understand the broad, interconnected impact of complex trauma. This can include children with social, emotional and mental health needs, disrupted relationships, instability in care or education, or difficulties with attachment, emotional regulation and trust.
The framework helps us build an individual picture rather than assuming trauma will affect every child in the same way.
What outcomes can AHCT help children achieve?
We want children to feel safer, develop trusting relationships and become more confident in regulating their emotions. As these foundations develop, children are often better able to engage in learning, form positive relationships and make meaningful academic and personal progress.
The aim is not to define children by their experiences. It is to understand their impact, recognise each child’s strengths and create the safety, relationships and opportunities they need to move forward.
How are parents and carers involved?
Families are a vital part of the team around a child. Parents and carers provide valuable insight into their child’s experiences, strengths, communication and behaviour. Their involvement continues through regular communication, reviews and TAC meetings.
Therapeutic Pastoral Leads can offer opportunities for discussion, support and collaboration. Information shared by families can complete the picture, while observations from school can help make sense of what is happening at home. Open communication gives children a more joined-up approach.
Ultimately, AHCT is about seeing the whole child and remaining curious about relationships, communication, emotional wellbeing, sensory needs, experiences, strengths and aspirations. When children feel safe, understood and valued, and the adults around them work together, we create the conditions for meaningful learning, growth and positive futures.
For some children, a specialist SEN school can provide the smaller, more personalised and therapeutic environment they need.
Could a therapeutic school help your child?
When children feel safe, understood and valued, they are better able to build relationships, engage with learning and move towards a positive future.
You can find your nearest Compass school to learn more about our specialist provision, or contact our team to discuss whether a therapeutic approach could meet your child’s needs.

Overcoming Childhood Trauma (OCT)
Helping Children Heal, Grow and Thrive
Overcoming Childhood Trauma (OCT) is Compass Community Schools’ specialist therapeutic programme designed to support children and young people who have experienced trauma, adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), loss or significant disruption in their early lives. The programme helps children understand their experiences, develop healthy coping strategies, build emotional resilience and regain confidence in themselves, their relationships and their education. At Compass Schools, we recognise that trauma can have a lasting impact on a child’s emotional wellbeing, behaviour, relationships and ability to learn. OCT combines therapeutic support, trauma-informed education and trusted relationships to help children move forward positively.
What Is Childhood Trauma?
Childhood trauma occurs when a child experiences events that feel overwhelming, frightening or unsafe. Experiences may include:
These experiences can affect how children see themselves, trust others and engage with learning. Many children who have experienced trauma may struggle with emotional regulation, anxiety, self-esteem, concentration, attendance or relationships with peers and adults.
Domestic abuse
Physical abuse
Emotional abuse
Sexual abuse
Household substance misuse
Family instability
Bereavement and loss
Placement breakdowns
Exposure to violence or conflict
How Does Trauma Affect Learning?
Trauma can impact brain development, emotional regulation and a child’s sense of safety. When children feel unsafe or overwhelmed, it can be difficult to:
This is why therapeutic education is so important. Before children can fully engage in learning, they often need support to feel safe, understood and emotionally regulated.
Concentrate in lessons
Retain information
Manage emotions
Build positive relationships
Cope with change and uncertainty
Participate confidently in school life
What Is the OCT Programme?
OCT is a structured therapeutic intervention that helps children explore and understand the impact of trauma in a safe, supportive and age-appropriate way. The programme combines:
Each programme is tailored to the individual needs, strengths and experiences of the child. The aim is not to focus on trauma itself, but to help children build resilience, develop healthier coping strategies and create a more positive future.
Individual therapeutic support

Relationship-based practice
Psychoeducation
Creative and child-centred approaches

Therapeutic Education and Trauma Recovery
At Compass Schools, therapy is not separate from education. Therapeutic thinking is embedded throughout the school day, helping children experience consistency, trust and emotional safety across every aspect of school life. Our therapeutic education model includes:
This joined-up approach helps children overcome barriers to learning and make progress both academically and emotionally.
Small class sizes

Who Can Benefit from OCT?
OCT may be suitable for children and young people who:
Support is always tailored to the individual child and their unique experiences.
Have experienced adverse childhood experiences (ACEs)
Have experienced trauma, loss or neglect
Present with SEMH needs
Experience anxiety or emotional dysregulation
Find relationships difficult
Have experienced disrupted education
Require therapeutic support alongside learning
Need a specialist therapeutic school environment
Why Choose Compass Schools?
Compass Schools are specialist therapeutic schools that combine personalised education, therapeutic support and trusted relationships to help children achieve positive futures. Through programmes such as OCT, we help children understand that their past experiences do not define their future. By creating safe environments where children feel valued and supported, we help them build confidence, resilience and a renewed enjoyment of learning.
Frequently Asked Questions
What does OCT stand for?
OCT stands for Overcoming Childhood Trauma. It is Compass Schools’ specialist therapeutic programme designed to help children and young people recover from the impact of trauma and adverse childhood experiences. What are adverse childhood experiences (ACEs)?
Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are potentially traumatic events that occur during childhood, such as abuse, neglect, domestic violence, parental substance misuse or significant family disruption. How does trauma-informed education help children?
Trauma-informed education recognises how trauma affects learning, behaviour and emotional wellbeing. It creates supportive environments where children feel safe, understood and able to succeed. Can children with SEMH needs benefit from OCT?
Yes. Many children with Social, Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH) needs have experienced adversity, trauma or disrupted relationships. OCT can help address underlying emotional needs while supporting educational progress. Is therapy provided in school?
Yes. At Compass Schools, therapeutic support is integrated into the school environment, allowing education and therapy professionals to work together to support each child’s wellbeing and learning.
